lesson.title: Strategic choices

steps.headline: Your best choice depends on what the other player does.

lead.text: A payoff matrix lists every pair of choices and what each player earns. To find your best response, fix your rival's choice and compare your own payoffs. A dominant strategy is a best response to every choice the rival might make.

reveal.text: You tested Alpha's best response against both of Beta's choices. When one strategy wins both times it is dominant, and Alpha needs no forecast of Beta.

lead.text: Alpha's payoffs are in the matrix. For each of Beta's choices, find which price pays Alpha more.

steps.headline: A Nash equilibrium is an outcome where nobody gains by switching alone.

lead.text: In a Nash equilibrium each player's choice is a best response to the other's, so a lone switch never helps. If it leaves both worse off than another outcome they could reach, the game is a prisoner's dilemma.

steps.headline: Price war: Alpha and Beta each choose High or Low. Find the Nash equilibrium.

workedSteps.text: Find Alpha's best response to each of Beta's choices.
workedSteps.math: Against High: Low pays 14, High pays 10. Against Low: Low pays 5, High pays 2.

workedSteps.text: Beta's payoffs mirror Alpha's, so Low is Beta's best response as well.
Both play Low, and each earns 5.

steps.headline: Two makers each choose plug standard A or B. Matching on A pays 6 each; matching on B pays 4 each; a mismatch pays nothing. Find the Nash equilibria.

workedSteps.text: At A/A, suppose Maker A switches alone to B while Maker B stays on A.
That is below the 6 A earned, so A/A is an equilibrium. B/B works the same way: a lone switch drops a maker from 4 to nothing.
A mismatched cell is not an equilibrium: a maker there earns nothing and gains by switching.
Count the cells where neither maker gains by switching alone.

reveal.text: Both choose Low and earn £5m each, £10m together, though High/High would give £20m. Each firm's best choice leaves both worse off: a prisoner's dilemma.

lead.text: Back in the price war, both firms play their dominant strategy. Look up what each earns there and add the two together.

reveal.text: Alpha is undercut once, then matches Low: £22m, while Beta earns £34m. Against another tit-for-tat player Alpha would earn £10m a round. When a game repeats, the threat of retaliation can make cooperation pay.

lead.text: Now the same firms meet for five rounds. Alpha plays tit for tat: High first, then it copies Beta's last move. Beta always sets Low.

cases.label: Tit for tat v always Low
Tit for tat v tit for tat

lesson.orientation: Find best responses, dominant strategies and Nash equilibria in payoff matrices, and see how repetition supports cooperation.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two rival firms each set a High or a Low price. What one earns depends on what the other does.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find best responses and equilibria in a payoff matrix, and say why repetition can make cooperation pay.

recap.keyIdea: Your best choice depends on the other player's. A Nash equilibrium is where nobody gains by switching alone, and it can leave everyone worse off, as in a prisoner's dilemma. Repetition can make cooperation pay, because a rival can punish.

blocks.text: You found Low dominant for both firms, £10m between them instead of £20m. A tit-for-tat Alpha still earned £22m against a rival who always cut.

recap.nextHook: Every lesson so far held something fixed. Try the tools together on a market you know.

questions.prompt: Alpha and Beta each set a High or Low price. If Beta sets High, Alpha earns £10m by also setting High and £14m by setting Low. If Beta sets Low, Alpha earns £2m with High and £5m with Low. When Beta sets High, how many £m more does Alpha earn by choosing Low?
hints: Fix Beta's choice and look only at that column.
Compare Alpha's two payoffs in it.
Subtract the smaller from the larger.
questions.onCorrect: £4m. To find a best response, fix the rival's choice and compare your own payoffs.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Alpha's payoff from Low, not the extra it earns over High.
That is Alpha's payoff from High. Find the difference between the two.
That compares the two payoffs in Beta's Low column. Beta sets High here.

questions.prompt: In that game Alpha earns £10m or £14m against High (setting High or Low) and £2m or £5m against Low. Which price is a dominant strategy for Alpha? Answer High or Low.
hints: Find Alpha's best response to each of Beta's choices.
A dominant strategy is the best response to every choice the rival makes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Low: it pays Alpha more whatever Beta does.

questions.onCorrect: Low. It pays more against High (£14m to £10m) and against Low (£5m to £2m).

misconceptions.feedback: High pays best only if Beta also sets High. A dominant strategy has to win against both of Beta's choices.

questions.prompt: In that game both firms play their dominant strategy (Low) and each earns £5m; both choosing High would give them £20m together. What combined profit, in £m, do the firms earn at the Nash equilibrium?
hints: Find the cell where both play their dominant strategy.
Read both payoffs in that cell.
Add them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Low/Low gives £5m + £5m = £10m, half the £20m of High/High.

questions.onCorrect: £10m. Both play Low, earning £5m each, half of the £20m that High/High would give.

misconceptions.feedback: That is each firm's profit. The question asks for the combined profit.
That is the combined profit at High/High, which is not the equilibrium.

questions.prompt: The firms play that game for five rounds. Alpha plays tit for tat (High in round one, then copies Beta's last move); Beta always sets Low. With payoffs of £2m for a lone High, £14m for a lone Low and £5m each for Low/Low, what is Alpha's total profit, in £m?
hints: Write down both moves for each round.
In round one only Alpha sets High.
Add Alpha's payoff across all five rounds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Round one: Alpha High, Beta Low, so Alpha earns £2m. Rounds two to five: Low/Low, £5m each. Total 2 + 4 × 5 = £22m.

questions.onCorrect: £22m. One undercut costs Alpha once; after that it matches Low and loses little more.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Beta's total. Alpha earns less.
That treats all five rounds as Low/Low. In round one Alpha plays High.
That is what Alpha would earn if Beta cooperated every round. Beta always sets Low.

hints: Check each of the four cells in turn.
In each cell, ask whether either maker gains by switching alone.
Count the cells where neither does.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A/A and B/B are both equilibria: in each, switching alone drops a maker to nothing. The mismatched cells are not.

questions.onCorrect: 2 equilibria. A/A and B/B are both stable; the mismatched cells are not.

misconceptions.feedback: Check every cell, not just the best-paying one.
The mismatched cells are not equilibria: a maker there earns nothing and gains by switching.

questions.prompt: A game in which each player's dominant strategy leaves both worse off than cooperation is called the prisoner's what? One word.
hints: Picture two suspects questioned separately, each tempted to confess.
questions.onCorrect: Dilemma. Each player's best choice leaves both worse off than cooperating.

misconceptions.feedback: A paradox is a puzzle; this one is a choice that tempts each player. The word is the one used for the two suspects.

questions.prompt: A player earns more from one strategy than from the other whatever the rival does. What is that strategy called?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A strategy that beats the alternative against every rival choice is dominant.

hints: Think about whether the rival's choice matters to this strategy.
questions.onCorrect: A dominant strategy: best against every choice the rival might make, so no forecast is needed.

misconceptions.feedback: A Nash equilibrium needs both players' choices. One player's strategy can be dominant on its own.
A dilemma describes the outcome for both players. Dominant describes one player's strategy.

questions.prompt: In a Nash equilibrium, which is true?

choices.label: Neither player gains by changing only their own choice.
Both players earn as much as they possibly can.
Both players choose the same strategy.

acceptedIdeas: Neither player gains by changing only their own choice.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A Nash equilibrium is a pair of best responses, so a lone switch never helps.

hints: What test defines an equilibrium?
questions.onCorrect: Each choice is a best response to the other's, so a lone switch never helps.

misconceptions.feedback: An equilibrium can leave both worse off than another outcome. It only rules out gains from switching alone.
Players can choose different strategies in an equilibrium. The test is whether switching alone helps.

questions.prompt: Why is Low/Low an equilibrium even though High/High pays more?

choices.label: Switching alone to High would cut a firm's own profit, so neither wants to move first.
Low pays more than High in every cell.

acceptedIdeas: Switching alone to High would cut a firm's own profit, so neither wants to move first.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: If Alpha alone switches to High it earns less than it does at Low/Low, and the same holds for Beta.

hints: What happens to one firm's profit if only that firm switches?
questions.onCorrect: A lone switch lowers the switcher's own profit, so neither moves, even though both would gain by moving together.

misconceptions.feedback: Low does not pay more in every cell. It pays more against each choice the rival makes.
High/High is allowed. It is simply not stable, because each firm gains by undercutting.

questions.prompt: Maker A's payoff after switching alone

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A mismatch pays nothing to either maker.

hints: Look at the cell where A has switched and B has not.
Read Maker A's payoff in that cell.
A mismatch pays nobody.
questions.onCorrect: Nothing. A lone switch from A/A falls into a mismatched cell.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what A earned before switching. Read the mismatched cell.
That is what both earn at B/B. Maker B has not moved.

questions.prompt: Rita picks a row and Cal a column. Payoffs in £m, as (Rita, Cal): Up/Left (5, 5), Up/Right (1, 7), Down/Left (7, 1), Down/Right (3, 3). Each player has a dominant strategy. What combined payoff do they earn at the Nash equilibrium, in £m?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Down beats Up for Rita against both columns, and Right beats Left for Cal against both rows. Down/Right pays (3, 3): 6 together.

hints: Find Rita's best response to each of Cal's choices.
Do the same for Cal.
Add both payoffs in the cell where both play their best response.
questions.onCorrect: £6m. Both play their dominant strategies, landing at Down/Right.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the combined payoff if both cooperated, which is not stable.
That is each player's payoff. The question asks for the combined payoff.

questions.prompt: The firms play four rounds. Alpha plays tit for tat (High first, then copying Beta's last move) and Beta always sets Low. A lone High pays £2m and Low/Low pays £5m each. What is Alpha's total profit, in £m?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Round one: Alpha High, Beta Low, so £2m. Rounds two to four: Low/Low, £5m each. 2 + 3 × 5 = £17m.

hints: Write both moves for each round.
In round one only Alpha sets High.
Add Alpha's payoff across the four rounds.
questions.onCorrect: £17m. One round as the sucker, then Low/Low for the rest.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats every round as Low/Low. In round one Alpha plays High.
That is the total for five rounds. Count four.
